source.title: Scaling in Cognitive Modelling: a Multilingual Approach to Human Reading Times
source.citation: Andrea Gregor de Varda et al., 2023
source.authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda; M. Marelli

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different outcome from pretraining loss: how well surprisal from differently sized language models predicts human reading times. This conceptually tests downstream predictability, not the original held-out-loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The study compares psychological fit across four XGLM sizes and reports relationships between perplexity and fit. It does not test power-law held-out loss, small-run extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or architectural-shape effects. Table 1 reports surprisal coefficients by language, model, and eye measure, but these are not the study's model-fit comparison measure; the relevant scale comparison is reported in Figure 1.
record.test_reason: The study asks whether a downstream use of LM outputs improves with scale: how well surprisal predicts human reading times. It compares four XGLM sizes (564M–4.5B) on eye-tracking data in ten languages. It frames cognitive modelling as a possible exception to scaling laws, so it is a new-setting test of V6 (T3), not a different method on the same measure (T2).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Larger XGLM models give surprisal that is less predictive of early eye-tracking measures (FF, GD). The authors say this corroborates cognitive modelling as an exception to scaling laws. For total reading time, a relatively larger but not the largest model (1.7B) fits best. They conclude that the best model size depends on the complexity of the processing stage measured.
record.recipe_differences: Uses four pre-trained XGLM sizes and compares their psychometric fit on multilingual eye-tracking data, rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The result varies by eye-tracking measure: the size pattern differs between FF/GD and TT, and the perplexity–fit relationship is near-linear for FF, nonlinear for GD, and nonsignificant for TT.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2023
record.problems: The model sample is limited to four sizes from one multilingual family, as the authors note. Figure 1 values are not given numerically in the text. The reported cross-size outcomes concern reading-time fit, not held-out loss or compute.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports surprisal regression coefficients, t statistics, and p-values by language, model, and eye measure. These are not the study's stated cross-model psychological-fit metric (∆LogLik), so they were not entered as separate rows.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Extrapolation of fitted laws to larger runs: not done.
Effect of depth/width at fixed size: not studied.
Other modalities or training regimes: not studied.
Only reading-time psychometric fit is tested, with one model family over less than one order of magnitude (564M–4.5B). Standard NLP downstream tasks are not tested.
Exponents and fitting choices: not studied.

missing.what: Numeric ∆LogLik per model and measure: Figure 1 gives only box plots of language-standardized values, and no numbers appear in the text.

record.verdict_notes: Psychometric fit of surprisal is a downstream use of LM predictions, so it is linked to V6. However, the authors use parameter count as a stand-in for linguistic accuracy rather than measuring held-out loss. Their perplexity is per-text and confounded across languages. Scale range is narrow: four sizes from one family. Table 1 coefficients are properly declared as left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling laws in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests prediction of human eye-movement reading times only, using XGLM models and the MECO-L1 data; it does not test other downstream tasks or establish general predictability from pretraining loss.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and their dependence on parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method.

rows.subject: XGLM models (four-model family; aggregate relationship)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a generalized additive mixed model relating perplexity to ∆LogLik, with random slopes and intercepts for language.

conditions.value: perplexity and ∆LogLik relationship across models, with language random effects

rows.value: Significant relationship: EDF = 6.093, F = 3.623, p = 0.0095; graphically positive and (near)-linear
rows.note: The authors say this supports a negative relationship between linguistic and psychological accuracy for FF: higher perplexity is associated with higher fit.
rows.check: State is correct: higher perplexity goes with higher fit. Note that this perplexity is per-text and not cleanly comparable across languages; the authors partly mitigate this with language random effects.

rows.subject: XGLM models (four-model family; aggregate relationship)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a generalized additive mixed model relating perplexity to ∆LogLik, with random slopes and intercepts for language.

conditions.value: perplexity and ∆LogLik relationship across models, with language random effects

rows.value: Significant partial effect: EDF = 6.760, F = 4.466, p = 0.0019; nonlinear, with growth, a plateau, and trend inversions
rows.note: The authors describe an initial increase, a plateau, and inversions, including one in the 400–550 perplexity range and another in the 500–600 range.
rows.check: The GD perplexity–fit curve rises with perplexity at first, opposite to V6, then plateaus and inverts. The authors call it 'less clear-cut'. Partial is defensible only as 'mixed'. Perplexity here is computed per eye-tracking text with language-dependent effective vocabularies, not held-out pretraining loss.

relationships.condition: First fixation duration, XGLM 564M–4.5B, ten languages
relationships.reason: Fit gained from surprisal falls as size grows, with the smallest model best (r1–r4). Higher perplexity is significantly associated with higher fit (p=0.0095, r13).
relationships.display_finding: Surprisal-based fit declined with model size, with the smallest model performing best and higher perplexity significantly associated with better fit at p=0.0095.

relationships.reason: The text reports the same decreasing-with-size trend as FF (r5–r8). The perplexity–fit relation is significant but nonlinear, rising with perplexity at first (r14).
relationships.display_finding: Fit declined with model size, while its significant relationship with perplexity was nonlinear and initially increased with perplexity.

relationships.condition: Total reading time, XGLM 564M–4.5B, ten languages
relationships.reason: The intermediate 1.7B model gives the highest mean fit, so the size trend is non-monotonic (r9–r12). The perplexity–fit relation is non-significant (p=0.123, r15).
relationships.display_finding: The 1.7B model achieved the highest mean fit, and the perplexity–fit relationship was nonsignificant (p=0.123).
